title: Transport Systems in Living Things
seo_title: Secondary 2 Science: Transport Systems in Humans and Plants Worksheets with Answers
standard_code: Secondary 2: Transport Systems in Living Things
standard_text: Describe the functions of arteries, veins and capillaries and of xylem and phloem; explain the need for transport systems in multicellular organisms; explain how diffusion moves digested food and oxygen in humans and gases and mineral salts in plants, and that osmosis helps roots absorb water; recognise the harmful effects of drug abuse and ethical issues in heart transplants (summary of the MOE Lower Secondary Science Syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 2 science worksheets for Singapore students on transport systems: arteries, veins and capillaries, xylem and phloem, diffusion, osmosis and surface area to volume ratio. With answers.
key_big: Diffusion is too slow for a large body.
key_sub: Arteries away, veins back; xylem water, phloem food.
body_html:
How to think about it

Large organisms need transport systems because diffusion alone is too slow.

  • Arteries carry blood away from the heart (thick walls, high pressure). Veins carry blood back (valves). Capillaries are one cell thick for exchange.
  • Xylem carries water and mineral salts up from the roots. Phloem carries food (sugars) from the leaves.
  • Oxygen and digested food reach cells by diffusion. Water enters root hairs by osmosis.
  • Drug abuse can damage the heart and blood vessels.
Example

Which vessel carries blood back to the heart?

It has valves

Answer: a vein

Example

A celery stalk in red water: where does the red go?

Water travels up

Answer: the xylem

Common mistakes

  • Saying veins carry blood away from the heart.
  • Saying xylem carries food. Xylem carries water; phloem carries food.
  • Thinking diffusion alone is enough for a large body.
  • Saying water enters roots by diffusion of salt. It enters by osmosis.

faq.q: What is the difference between arteries and veins?
faq.a: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure and have thick walls. Veins carry blood back to the heart and have valves.

faq.q: What do xylem and phloem carry?
faq.a: Xylem carries water and mineral salts from the roots. Phloem carries food made in the leaves.

faq.q: How does water enter a plant's roots?
faq.a: By osmosis, through the partially permeable membranes of root hair cells.

items.q: Why are root hair cells long and thin?
c: to give a large surface area for absorbing water and mineral salts
items.e: They have no chloroplasts.

items.q: Water moves up from the roots to the leaves of a balsam plant. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Kavya put a white daisy in blue-coloured water for a day. What does the experiment show?
c: Food is carried down to the roots.
Leaves take in water from the air.
Water is carried up the stem to the leaves and flowers.
items.e: The colour travels with the water.

items.q: A ring of the outer layer of bark was removed from the trunk of a young tree (ring-barking). After some weeks, the trunk just above the ring swelled. Why?
c: The tree grew new roots there.
Food carried down from the leaves collected above the ring.
items.e: The phloem were cut, so food could not pass the ring.

items.q: Sugar made in the leaves is carried to the fruits of a durian tree. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Nurul put a white chrysanthemum in blue-coloured water for a day. The stem was then cut across. What do the coloured spots show?

items.e: The colour travels with the water.

items.q: A ring of the outer layer of bark was removed from the trunk of a young tree (ring-barking). What happens to the roots?
c: They do not get food and slowly die.
items.e: Roots cannot make food; they depend on the phloem.

items.q: Sugars move from the leaves to the growing shoot tip. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: A ring of the outer layer of bark was removed from the trunk of a young tree (ring-barking). Which part of the tree swells?
c: the part just above the ring
the part just below the ring
items.e: Food moving down cannot pass the ring.

items.q: Which tubes carry sugar to a ripening mango?
items.e: The phloem carry food from the leaves to the other parts.

items.q: A ring of the outer layer of bark was removed from the trunk of a young tree (ring-barking). Can the leaves still make food?
c: No, the leaves die at once.
No, the leaves need the bark to make food.
Yes, for a time, because they still get water and light.
items.e: The problem is that the food cannot reach the roots.

items.q: How does water enter a root hair cell?
c: by osmosis, from the soil water into the cell
items.e: The root hair gives a large surface area.

items.q: Food made in the leaves is stored in the tubers of a tapioca plant. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Zhi Hao put a balsam plant in red-coloured water for a day. Why would the colour move up faster on a hot, windy day?
c: More water is lost from the leaves, so more water is drawn up.
items.e: Water loss from the leaves pulls water up the stem.

items.q: A ring of bark is removed from a tree and the bark above the ring swells with sugar. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Which tubes carry food down to the roots?
items.e: The phloem carry food from the leaves to the other parts.

items.q: Which tubes carry food made in the leaves?
items.e: The phloem carry food from the leaves to the other parts.

items.q: Red dye rises up a celery stalk placed in red-coloured water. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Which tubes carry water to the leaves for making food?
items.e: The xylem carry water and mineral salts from the roots to the other parts.

items.q: Why does the blood in an artery spurt out when it is cut, but blood in a vein flows out slowly?

The leaves make too much food.

items.q: How can drug abuse harm the transport system?
